title: AI’s next constraint is megawatts, not GPUs (IEA, ERCOT, PJM)
summary: Everyone’s modeling AI demand in terms of chips. The gating factor showing up in the data is electricity. The IEA’s 2025 work pegs global data-center consumption at roughly 945 TWh by 2030 - about double today and just under 3% of world electricity. They also put the growth pace around 15%/yr through 2030, with the U.S. driving the largest share. That’s not a vibe; it’s a load curve.You can see the strain show up in prices where AI clusters. In PJM, the latest capacity auction printed $16.1B, up $7.3B (+82%) vs. the prior auction, and the market monitor said data centers were the primary reason. That’s a concrete cost of scarcity for tenants who thought "power later" was a viable plan."Just add more grid" isn’t fast. LBNL’s Queued Up 2024 shows the typical project that reached COD in 2023 took ~5 years from interconnection request - up from <2 years in the 2000s. In the meantime, the queue itself is multi-terawatt. The takeaway: utility interconnects don’t match AI deployment timelines.Regional forecasts underline the same thing. ERCOT is now working off scenarios where Texas data centers add ~35 GW by 2035 - a massive slice of the system. Nationally, BNEF has U.S. data-center load more than doubling to ~78 GW by 2035. Regardless of your view on AI valuations, the power leg of the buildout still has room to run.For investors, the frame I’m using is time-to-power. When capacity markets reprice scarcity and grid queues stretch, the economic value shifts to anything that compresses "months to megawatts": behind-the-meter microgrids, storage, fast-track interconnects, long-lead electrical equipment (transformers/switchgear), and developers who can actually deliver SLAs on schedule. Tenants that can bring firm, dispatchable power to site - or hedge peaks with storage - have a real advantage when everyone else is waiting on utilities.Risks? Sure: if the macro or an AI inventory glut slows buildouts, demand could undershoot. The IEA’s "headwind" scenario trims that 2030 data-center number materially. Local siting, water/cooling rules, and fuel costs also matter. But the base case is still tight power where AI clusters, and that pushes capital toward onsite solutions.I don’t have positions to disclose here. If you’re mapping the space, keep an eye on time-to-power integrators in microgrids and fleet-energy - think "bring your own megawatts" while the grid catches up.
